title: A given generic isomorphism from a semiabelian model is an open immersion
statement: Let $R$ be a discrete valuation ring [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring], $F=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ and $T=\operatorname{Spec}R$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Let $A\to T$ be a smooth separated commutative group scheme of finite presentation [def-pc-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation] with semiabelian geometric fibres [def-sfb-semiabelian-geometric-fibres]. Let $B\to T$ be any smooth separated commutative group scheme, without a quasi-compactness or finite-type assumption on $B$. A commutative group scheme has multiplication, inverse and identity morphisms satisfying the commutative group identities; separated means that its diagonal is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Suppose a $T$-group homomorphism $a:A\to B$ is given and that its generic base change $a_F:A\times_T\operatorname{Spec}F\to B\times_T\operatorname{Spec}F$ [def-pc-base-change] is an isomorphism. Then $a$ is an open immersion [def-weil-open-immersion]. No completeness, excellence or residue-field perfection hypothesis is imposed on $R$.

source.place: Agent generalization of Brian Conrad, Semistable reduction for abelian varieties, proof of Theorem 4.4, printed pp.12–16, especially Corollary 3.3, Lemma 4.9 and the quasi-finite birational argument. Local copy WANTED; primary lecture notes read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/DarmonCM/2011Notes/SemistableReduction.pdf . The theorem as printed has abelian generic fibre and Néron target; this statement extracts the proof for a GIVEN generically isomorphic homomorphism, where only smoothness and separatedness of the target are used. It is an agent-extracted lemma, not a verbatim assertion of Theorem 4.4.

proof.text: Fix a uniformizer $\pi$ and put $k=R/(\pi)$. Finite presentation of $A/T$ implies finite type directly from the finite polynomial presentations and quasi-compactness. The graph $\gamma=(1_A,a):A\to A\times_T B$ is the pullback of the closed diagonal of $B/T$ along $(a\operatorname{pr}_A,\operatorname{pr}_B):A\times_TB\to B\times_TB$. Thus $\gamma$ is a closed immersion by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-base-change], hence proper by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-fp-permanence](c), hence of finite type by [def-weil-proper-morphism]. The projection $A\times_TB\to B$ is of finite type by [lem-sfb-finite-type-composition-base-change](2); its composite with $\gamma$ is $a$, so (1) of that node makes $a$ of finite type. Likewise $\Delta_a$ is the pullback of $\Delta_{A/T}$ along $A\times_BA\to A\times_TA$. It is closed, so $a$ is separated. None of these assertions requires $B/T$ quasi-compact.

source.place: Tags 01KS (schemes-lemma-semi-diagonal), 01W1 (definition-proper), and 01T3 (lemma-composition-finite-type); graph and relative diagonal pullback squares written out.

proof.text: The generic group $A_F$ is integral. Indeed over an algebraic closure $\overline F$, its prescribed semiabelian exact sequence [def-sfb-semiabelian-geometric-fibres] satisfies [lem-sfb-semiabelian-geometric-power-integrality] with $n=1$, so $(A_F)_{\overline F}$ is integral. For every nonempty affine open $\operatorname{Spec}C\subseteq A_F$, the tensor map $C\to C\otimes_F\overline F$ is injective: choose an $F$-basis of $\overline F$ containing $1$ and project to that coordinate. The same coordinate decomposition shows $C\otimes_F\overline F\ne0$. This is the coordinate ring of a nonempty affine open in the integral base change, hence is a domain; its subring $C$ is a domain. The identity supplies nonemptiness, so [def-pc-integral-scheme] proves the claim. The given isomorphism $a_F$ therefore makes $B_F$ integral too.

source.place: Generic-fibre integrality in Conrad Theorem 4.4 proof, printed p.12; elementary faithful field-extension descent spelt out.

proof.text: By [lem-pc-smooth-flat], $A/T$ and $B/T$ are flat. Multiplication by $\pi$ is injective on $R$. At a point over the closed point, tensor this injection with the flat local ring using [def-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map]; at a point over the generic point, $\pi$ is a unit. Thus multiplication by $\pi$ is injective on every stalk of either structure sheaf [def-weil-flat-morphism], hence on sections of every open. For any nonempty affine $U=\operatorname{Spec}C$ of either scheme, the generic restriction is $U_F=D(\pi)=\operatorname{Spec}C[1/\pi]$. The localization map $C\to C[1/\pi]$ is injective since $C$ has no $\pi$-power torsion. In particular $U_F$ is nonempty and its coordinate ring is a domain by step 2. Hence $C$ is a domain. The identity sections and [def-pc-integral-scheme] now show that both $A$ and $B$ are integral, and every nonempty affine open meets the generic fibre. In particular the generic fibres are dense.

source.place: Conrad proof of Theorem 4.4, printed p.12; DVR-flatness argument made explicit on stalks and affine localizations.

proof.text: The ring $R$ is a principal ideal domain by [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring], so [lem-weil-pbc-pid-noetherian-normal] makes it normal. Each $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is normal by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-normal-domain]; these are the local rings of $T$ by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-open-stalk-localization]. Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-normal-ascent] to the smooth map $B\to T$. Thus every local ring of the integral scheme $B$ is integrally closed. This uses neither excellence nor completion.

Choose a prime $\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k$; its image in the local ring $R$ is a unit. Set $E=A[\ell]$, $D=B[\ell]$, the kernels of multiplication by $\ell$. By [lem-sfb-smooth-group-invertible-multiplication] both are etale over $T$, and their formation commutes with base change. These are schemes because they are the scheme fibre products defining the kernels. The group homomorphism $a$ induces $u:E\to D$. Since $E$ and $D$ are etale over $T$, [lem-trf-space-chartwise-etale-permanence] implies $u$ is etale (take schemes as their represented algebraic spaces). Its kernel $L=E\times_{D,u,e_D}T$ is etale over $T$ by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-scheme-base-change]. The scheme $L$ is separated over $T$: $E$ is closed in $A$, since it is the pullback of the closed identity section of $A$ under $[\ell]_A$, and $L$ is closed in $E$ in the same way using $D\subset B$. Identity sections of separated groups are closed because a section is the pullback of the diagonal. The closed-immersion base-change assertion applies to all these squares. Closed immersions are proper, hence separated, and separated morphisms compose by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-fp-permanence](c),(e).

source.place: Conrad proof of Theorem 4.4, printed pp.13–14 (invertible torsion); Stacks Tags 02GW (lemma-etale-permanence), 02GO (lemma-base-change-etale).

proof.text: The identity section $e_L:T\to L$ is also open. Indeed $L/T$ is unramified by [lem-sfb-space-unramified-permanence], so its diagonal is open by [lem-sfb-space-unramified-diagonal-open]; pulling it back along $(1_L,e_Lp):L\to L\times_TL$ gives $e_L$. Thus $L=e_L(T)\amalg C$ for an open and closed complement $C$. On generic fibres $u_F$ is an isomorphism since $a_F$ is; hence $L_F=e_L(T)_F$ as schemes and $C_F=\varnothing$. Every stalk of $C$ is flat over the corresponding local ring of $T$, since $C$ is open in the etale $L$ [def-weil-etale-morphism]. If $x\in C$, its image must be the closed point and $\pi$ is a nonzerodivisor in the nonzero local ring $\mathcal O_{C,x}$: tensor the injection $R\xrightarrow{\pi}R$ using [def-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map]. But $C_F=\varnothing$ says that in an affine neighbourhood of $x$, inverting $\pi$ gives the zero ring, so some power of $\pi$ is zero there, a contradiction. Therefore $C=\varnothing$ and $e_L:T\xrightarrow{\sim}L$. This replaces the strict-henselian lifting diagram without assuming finiteness of $B[\ell]$.

source.place: Conrad Theorem 4.4, pp.13–14, torsion injectivity; agent expansion via the open diagonal (Stacks 02GE) and DVR torsion-freeness, avoiding a global quasi-finiteness hypothesis on B.

proof.text: Let $\Omega$ be any algebraically closed extension of $k$. Put $K_\Omega=\ker(a_\Omega:A_\Omega\to B_\Omega)$. This is a closed subgroup of $A_\Omega$: the kernel is the pullback of the closed identity section of the separated group $B_\Omega$. The group laws restrict because $a$ preserves them. The kernel of multiplication by $\ell$ in $K_\Omega$ is exactly $L_\Omega$: on every test scheme both classify points of $A_\Omega$ killed by $\ell$ and by $a_\Omega$, and the inverse fibre-product maps are induced by those same projections. By step 6 it is the trivial group scheme. The source $A_\Omega$ is smooth, separated and of finite type by base change, and is semiabelian by the hypothesis on geometric fibres. Apply [lem-sfb-semiabelian-closed-subgroup-trivial-torsion-finite]. It gives that $K_\Omega$ is finite over $\Omega$. This assertion allows a nonreduced kernel.

source.place: Conrad Corollary 3.3, printed p.8, applied as in the proof of Theorem 4.4, p.13.

proof.text: All fibres of $a$ have finite underlying sets. Generic-fibre points have singleton fibres because $a_F$ is an isomorphism. For a point $y$ in the special fibre of $B$, put $Q=A\times_B\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)$. If $Q$ is nonempty, choose a point $x\in Q$ and an algebraic closure $M$ of $\kappa(x)$. This makes $M$ an algebraically closed extension of $k$ and supplies $z\in Q(M)$. Translation gives mutually inverse scheme maps $Q_M\to K_M$, $w\mapsto w-z$, and $K_M\to Q_M$, $h\mapsto h+z$: the equations $a(w-z)=a(w)-a(z)=0$ and $a(h+z)=y$ hold on every test scheme, and the group identities give the two inverse composites. By step 7, $K_M$ is finite; [lem-weil-pbc-finite-closed-map-finite-fibres](2) therefore makes its underlying set finite. The map $\operatorname{Spec}M\to\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)$ is surjective, so [lem-weil-pbc-surjective-base-change] makes $Q_M\to Q$ surjective. Hence $|Q|$ is finite. Empty fibres cause no exception. Since $a$ is of finite type by step 1, [pqf-lem-locqf-fibre-discrete] makes it quasi-finite at every point, hence quasi-finite by [pqf-def-quasifinite].

source.place: Conrad Theorem 4.4 proof, pp.12–13, finite kernel implies finite fibres. The translation argument is written out for arbitrary locally finite type targets, avoiding the finite-type-target hypothesis of lem-sfb-finite-kernel-group-fibres.

proof.text: It remains to apply Zariski Main Theorem locally on $B$. Fix a nonempty affine open $V\subseteq B$ and put $X=a^{-1}(V)$. Restricting a finite-type separated map to a target open preserves these properties by the affine definition and the diagonal pullback square; the fibres remain finite. Thus $f:X\to V$ satisfies [pqf-lem-normalization-open] (the target $V$ is affine, hence quasi-compact and quasi-separated by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-scheme-qcqs]). Write its relative normalization factorization as $X\xrightarrow{j}N\xrightarrow{p}V$. That node gives that $j$ is an open immersion and $p$ is integral. The scheme $X$ is nonempty and integral: $V_F$ is nonempty by step 3, $X_F\simeq V_F$, and $X$ is an open of the integral $A$. Clause (iv) of [lem-weil-pbc-relative-normalization] therefore makes $N$ integral. The open $j(X)$ is nonempty, hence dense in integral $N$.

source.place: Stacks Tag 02LR (more-morphisms-lemma-quasi-finite-separated-quasi-affine) and 035H/035I (relative normalization); apply over each affine target open.

proof.text: The common nonempty opens $X_F\subseteq X$ and $V_F\subseteq V$ are isomorphic via $f_F$. Consequently $f$ maps the generic point of $X$ to that of $V$ and induces an isomorphism on their local rings. Since $j$ is an open immersion of nonempty integral schemes, it maps the generic point of $X$ to that of $N$ and induces an isomorphism on those same generic local rings. The identity $p\circ j=f$ therefore shows that $p$ maps the generic point of $N$ to that of $V$ and induces an isomorphism of function fields (generic local rings) [lem-sc-integral-function-field-affine-fraction]. Normality of $B$ from step 4 gives normal local rings on $V$. Apply [lem-trf-integral-birational-normal-isomorphism] to $p:N\to V$: it is an isomorphism. Thus $f=p\circ j$ identifies $X$ with an open subscheme of $V$. These identifications over affine opens of $B$ agree on intersections, because they are restrictions of the single map $a$; their inverses agree by uniqueness of inverses. They glue to an identification of $A$ with the open union of their images in $B$. By [def-weil-open-immersion], $a$ is an open immersion.

source.place: Stacks Tag 0AB1 (morphisms-lemma-finite-birational-over-normal), integral variant. Conrad Theorem 4.4, printed p.13, conclusion of Zariski Main Theorem argument.

reviewed.note: mechanical checks by tools/merge_delivery.py; mathematics reviewed in full by NT-cc-Q62-0d8fd9a59 (reviewer sub-agent of L); spot-checked: I read the item, the new node and the statements of all 39 cited nodes. All ten steps hold against the cited statements. Step 1: the graph is the pullback of the diagonal of B, which makes a of finite type and separated with no qc assumption on B. Steps 2-3: A_Fbar is integral by power-integrality with n=1, and flatness plus localization at pi makes A and B integral. Step 4: smooth-normal-ascent makes B normal. Steps 5-6: A[l] and B[l] are etale, so the kernel L is etale; its identity section is open (unramified diagonal) and closed, the generic fibre of the complement is empty, and pi-flatness forces the complement to be empty. Step 7: the special kernel is a closed subgroup whose l-torsion is L_Omega, which is trivial, and the new node then makes it finite. Step 8: explicit translations show the fibres are finite, without the finite-type-target lemma, so a is quasi-finite. Steps 9-10: ZMT over affine V with qcqs V, relative-normalization (iv) makes N integral, and integral-birational-normal makes p an isomorphism, which glues to an open immersion. The new node lem-sfb-semiabelian-closed-subgroup-trivial-torsion-finite (Conrad Cor. 3.3) is true: if dim H > 0 then (H_red)^0 is a nonzero semiabelian variety with nonzero l-torsion inside H[l]. It allows nonreduced H, is statement-only with all four search kinds recorded, and is not a duplicate of the invertible-multiplication, torsion-kernel-divisibility, prime-to-torsion-density or finite-kernel-group-fibres nodes, nor a restatement of a clause of the item. The parent's use of the item matches its statement and there is no cycle. The four tool_uses (chartwise-etale permanence, smooth base change, locqf fibre criterion, integral-birational-normal) are generic and accepted. Batch-5: I recomputed the closures. None reaches an nt-assume leaf, a trace-formula or PD theorem, or a batch-4 target; the trf and pod nodes in the closure are algebraic-space, fppf, etale and module foundations and definitions, so all six flags are accepted. Minor note: in step 2, commutativity of the abelian quotient is left implicit; it follows because the quotient is an fppf image of a commutative group. No fixes.
